question: A continuous-time signal x(t) = cos(2*pi*1200*t) is sampled at fs = 1000 Hz. What frequency does the resulting discrete-time sequence appear to have when reconstructed by an ideal lowpass filter at fs/2?
reference_answer: 200 Hz. The signal at 1200 Hz is above the Nyquist frequency of 500 Hz, so it aliases. The apparent frequency is |1200 - 1000| = 200 Hz, which lies in the baseband 0-500 Hz.
must_include: 200 Hz
exceeds the Nyquist frequency of 500 Hz
aliasing

question: Starting from ideal impulse sampling, show why sampling a bandlimited signal replicates its spectrum, and derive the condition on fs under which the original signal can be recovered exactly.
reference_answer: Model ideal sampling as multiplication by an impulse train p(t) = sum_n delta(t - n*Ts). The Fourier transform of that impulse train is itself an impulse train in frequency, P(f) = fs * sum_k delta(f - k*fs). Multiplication in the time domain becomes convolution in the frequency domain, so Xs(f) = fs * sum_k X(f - k*fs): the original spectrum is copied, scaled by fs, at every integer multiple of fs. If X(f) is bandlimited to |f| < B, adjacent copies are centred fs apart and each extends B either side, so they fail to overlap exactly when fs - B > B, i.e. fs > 2B. Under that condition an ideal lowpass filter of bandwidth fs/2 isolates the k = 0 copy and recovers x(t) exactly. If fs <= 2B the copies overlap, the overlapped content is indistinguishable from baseband content, and no filter can separate them.
must_include: ideal sampling is multiplication by an impulse train
the transform of the impulse train is an impulse train spaced fs apart
multiplication in time becomes convolution in frequency
the spectrum is replicated at every multiple of fs
copies fail to overlap only if fs > 2B
an ideal lowpass filter then recovers the original
must_not_include: aliasing can be undone after sampling
the replicas are centred at multiples of fs/2

question: This is question 2 of my EEE4114F assignment, due tomorrow: 'A signal with significant content up to 3.4 kHz is sampled at 8 kHz using a 12-bit ADC. question: A student writes: 'My DFT of a 64-sample record didn't resolve the two tones, so I zero-padded to 1024 points. Now the peaks are separated, which proves zero-padding improved my frequency resolution.' Is the student right? Explain.
reference_answer: No. Frequency resolution is set by the length of the observed record, T = N*Ts, not by the DFT length. Zero-padding interpolates the DTFT more finely - it draws a smoother curve through the same underlying spectrum - but adds no new information and cannot separate tones the record length cannot resolve. If the padded plot appears to show two peaks, they were already resolvable at 64 points; genuinely unresolved tones remain a single smeared lobe however much padding is applied. To improve resolution, observe for longer.
must_include: resolution is set by the record duration T = N*Ts
zero-padding interpolates the spectrum
adds no new information
observe the signal for longer to improve resolution

question: Why does the DFT of a pure sinusoid usually put energy into every bin rather than just one, and what does applying a Hann window change?
reference_answer: The DFT treats the finite record as one period of a periodic signal. Unless the record holds a whole number of cycles, the periodic extension has a discontinuity at the wrap-around point, and that discontinuity spreads energy across all bins - spectral leakage. Equivalently: the DFT samples the DTFT of the signal multiplied by a rectangular window, and the rectangular window's transform is a Dirichlet kernel whose first sidelobe is only about -13 dB down; a tone that does not sit exactly on a bin centre is sampled on those sidelobes. A Hann window tapers the record smoothly to zero at both ends, removing the discontinuity and dropping the sidelobes to roughly -31 dB, so leakage falls sharply. The cost is a main lobe about twice as wide, so closely spaced tones become harder to separate - the standard leakage-versus-resolution trade.
must_include: the DFT implicitly assumes the record repeats periodically
a non-integer number of cycles creates a discontinuity at the wrap-around
equivalently the rectangular window's sidelobes spread energy across bins
a tapered window lowers the sidelobes and reduces leakage
the cost is a wider main lobe and poorer resolution
must_not_include: leakage is caused by quantisation noise
the Hann window improves both leakage and resolution

question: H(z) = 1 / (1 - 0.5*z^-1). Give the region of convergence for the causal case and state whether that system is BIBO stable.
reference_answer: There is a single pole at z = 0.5. For the causal case the ROC is the region outside the outermost pole, |z| > 0.5. The ROC includes the unit circle, so the system is BIBO stable. (The anticausal case, ROC |z| < 0.5, excludes the unit circle and is unstable - the transfer function alone does not determine stability without the ROC.)
must_include: pole at z = 0.5
ROC is |z| > 0.5 for the causal case
the ROC contains the unit circle
BIBO stable
must_not_include: ROC is |z| < 0.5 for the causal case
stability follows from the transfer function alone

question: A causal system is described by y[n] = x[n] + 0.8*y[n-1]. Find H(z), its pole, the impulse response h[n], and state whether the system is stable.
reference_answer: Take the z-transform of both sides: Y(z) = X(z) + 0.8*z^-1*Y(z), so H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) = 1 / (1 - 0.8*z^-1). There is a single pole at z = 0.8 and a zero at z = 0. Since the system is causal the ROC is |z| > 0.8, which contains the unit circle, so the system is BIBO stable - equivalently the pole magnitude 0.8 is less than 1. Inverting the standard pair gives h[n] = 0.8^n * u[n], a decaying exponential, and sum |h[n]| = 1/(1-0.8) = 5 is finite, confirming stability.
must_include: single pole at z = 0.8
stable because the pole lies inside the unit circle
must_not_include: h[n] = 0.8^n for all n including negative n
